label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
# Dear Jonno, About the Coolroom

Jonno,

You've now messaged me about this four times, so here it is, once, in writing, and you can read it on the Tube or wherever it is you people go to be sad and damp.

Short version: the coolroom compressor died overnight on the Monday before Cup Day, I found it at 6.40am on the Tuesday, and the thermometer said 11 degrees. You know what it's meant to say. It's not 11.

Long version below, because I know you.

## 6.40am

I walk in, coffee in hand, feeling pretty good about life. Open the coolroom door and it's that warm, kind of sweet smell. Not hot, just wrong. Like the room has given up and is quietly thinking about its choices. I looked at the thermometer, looked at it again like it might change its mind, and said a word I won't put on the internet because my mum reads this.

Cup Day lunch was 140 covers. Set menu. Three courses. Everything we needed for it was sitting in a room that had been quietly cooking itself since sometime around midnight.

Raff was away, so it was me running the show. Which is a lovely thing to find out at 6.40 in the morning.

## Phil's plan

I rang Phil, because that's what you do. I explained the situation clearly and calmly. He listened and then said, and I'm quoting here, "just make it work mate."

That's it. That's the plan. Thank you Phil. Truly a visionary. You'd have loved it, you'd have done the impression for a week.

I also rang Wally from Coldline, who does our fridges. Wally was very nice about it and said he couldn't get out until Wednesday because the part had to come from Sydney. Wednesday. Cup Day was Tuesday. So the coolroom was officially a very large, very expensive cupboard.

## Operation Make It Work Mate

Here's what we had to work with: two undercounters, the bar fridge, and whatever space we could beg off the universe.

The universe, as it turns out, is a woman called Marta who runs the cafe next door. I went in there at about 7.15 looking like a man who'd lost a fight with a freezer, and she just said "take half the walk-in." No questions. Absolute legend. I now owe her in croissant credit, which Marta calculated, and I'm not exaggerating, as roughly three weeks of staff meal. I don't know how that maths works but I'm not in a position to argue. Start saving, because I'm not paying that on my own.

So the plan was: triage. Anything that could survive got shuffled into the undercounters and the bar fridge, which for the record is now holding more than any bar fridge should be asked to hold. Anything that couldn't survive went in the bin, and I'll get to that.

Everything big went next door.

## The beef shin

This is the bit you're going to be most upset you missed.

We had 30kg of beef shin that needed to get from our kitchen to Marta's walk-in. That means going out the back, down the laneway, and in her back door. In the rain, obviously, because Melbourne had read the script.

Me and Benny found a milk crate trolley. You know the one. The sort of contraption that was built for carrying milk crates and has never once been asked to carry 30kg of raw beef down a laneway in the rain.

We loaded it up and off we went, two grown men in aprons pushing a wet pile of meat down an alley like we were running some sort of very specific smuggling operation.

About halfway, one of the wheels fell off.

Just fell off. No warning. Benny looked at me, I looked at Benny, and neither of us said anything because there was nothing to say. We just picked up the corner and kept going, dragging the whole thing like a broken shopping trolley, rain coming down, beef shin sliding around on the crate.

And this is where table 9 comes in, because later on a lady sitting at the window had clearly watched this whole thing go past. When she got her main, she asked the waiter whether the beef was, and again I'm quoting, "free range from the laneway."

I'd like to formally say yes. Yes it was. Artisanal. Hand-delivered. Laneway-raised.

## Ice

Meanwhile, Dishy Kev, who is a hero and who I will never say that to his face, took it upon himself to fill our old esky with ice. He went to the servo and bought ice. Fourteen bags. Fourteen.

The guy at the servo asked him if we were having a party.

Kev said, "Something like that."

I'd have paid good money to see his face. Fourteen bags of ice at a servo on Cup Day morning is a statement. That man looked at Kev and saw a person with plans.

## The damage

At the end of all the triage, here's what we lost: about $1,800 of stock. Mostly dairy and the duck legs. The duck legs hurt. I'd like to hold a small service for the duck legs.

That's not a catastrophe, it's an annoying number, and it's a lot better than it could've been. If I'd walked in at 8 instead of 6.40, or if Marta had said no, or if Kev hadn't gone full ice baron, we'd have been in real trouble. As it was, the number was bad but the lunch was fine.

## The panna cotta

At 12.15, mid-service, I had to 86 the panna cotta.

If you were here you'd know that's not nothing. It was the dessert on the set menu, and on a set menu you don't really get to take things off. It's three courses, everyone's having the same three courses, and now one of them is gone.

So we improvised. Dessert became "affogato with whatever," and I'm going to be honest with you because I know you'll hate this: people loved it more.

Genuinely. I don't know what that says about the panna cotta, or about me, or about the whole concept of planning a menu in advance. But table after table, people were thrilled. Someone said it was the best dessert they'd had all year. We had not planned it. We had not tested it. It was, in the most literal sense, whatever.

I'm choosing not to think about it too hard.

## The sweep

Now, because the universe has a sense of humour, I should also tell you about the sweep.

I picked a horse. Of course I did, it's Cup Day. My horse was called Ice Cold Lad.

Ice Cold Lad. On the day the coolroom died. I swear to you I didn't do it on purpose, it was drawn out of a hat. And he came second last.

The universe is taking the piss, mate. There's no other explanation.

## Why I'm telling you this

Here's the thing, and don't let it go to your head.

It was the best service we did all year.

I don't know how else to say it. Everyone was locked in. Nobody was whinging, nobody was standing around, nobody had time to be in a mood. We had no coolroom and 140 people to feed, and for some reason that made everyone better at their job. Benny and the beef, Kev and the ice, the floor team handling a changed dessert like it was always meant to be that way. It was loud and chaotic and a bit unhinged, and it just worked.

That's the thing about bistro kitchens. They don't run on money or planning or proper equipment. They run on bar fridges and spite.

You know that. You used to know that. You were on grill with me for how long? You knew exactly what it felt like when everything's going sideways and everyone just gets on with it.

Now you live in London, and I'm pretty sure you've gone soft. I reckon if you'd been here that morning, you'd have walked into the coolroom, seen the thermometer, and cried. Actual tears. I'm not even being mean, I just know you. You've been drinking flat whites in a city with a Pret on every corner and you've lost it.

Wally fixed the compressor on the Wednesday, by the way. Part came from Sydney, he put it in, and the coolroom has been behaving itself ever since. I still walk in every morning and check the thermometer like it owes me money.

So that's what happened. Now you know. You can stop messaging me.

Come home, ya flog.

---

*Wasn't going to write this post at all. Jonno made me.*

---

I left Raff just "away" with no reason, so his dad's stuff stays out of it. If you want that last italic line gone, it's easy to cut, and the Coldline bit and Phil's quote are the other things worth a glance in case you'd rather soften them.
